# OWASP GenAI Security Project, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026

**Source:** OWASP GenAI Security Project, *OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026*, Version 2026, dated August 4th, 2026 on the cover; Project Lead Steve Wilson, Co-Lead Rock Lambros; genai.owasp.org. Licence CC BY-SA 4.0. Scope: open.
**Structure:** 122 pages. A letter from the project leads on method, a What's New section, and Moving Forward (pp. 5–8); ten risk entries, LLM01 to LLM10, each with a description, common examples, prevention and mitigation strategies, and attack scenarios (pp. 10–57); Appendix A consolidating the ten entries' mappings to nine external frameworks (pp. 58–105); Appendix B on architecture and threat modeling, carried in images apart from its title (pp. 106–107); references grouped by entry, acknowledgements, sponsors and supporters (pp. 108–122).

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The project leads' posture, which they say runs through all ten entries, is to stop trying to build a model that cannot be fooled and to build the system around it so that, when it is fooled, nothing important breaks (p. 5). For the first time the practitioner vote behind the list was tested against an incident record: 7,714 real incidents from public vulnerability databases and an AI-harm database, of which classifiers placed the 6,639 with enough detail to sort (p. 5). Where vote and record diverged, the leads say the disagreements taught them more than the agreements; the vote carries three-quarters of the weight and the incident data a quarter, enough to move an entry a tier where belief and evidence diverge widely, but not to rewrite the list on its own (p. 5).

The entries turn that posture into engineering guidance. Prompt injection is intrinsic to current generative AI and has no reliable prevention today, so defense is architectural: constrain what the model may do and what its outputs may reach (LLM01, p. 13). Authorization belongs in deterministic logic outside the model (LLM03, p. 25; LLM08, p. 48); hidden context should be assumed discoverable (LLM08, p. 46); model output should be treated like input from any other user (LLM10, p. 56). The list covers the model as a component of an application; once the model acts, with tools, memory and downstream consequences, the risk moves to the OWASP Agentic Top 10, which entries should be paired with (p. 7).

## Method and What Changed in 2026

Prompt injection stays first although the raw incident record would drop it out of the top 10; the leads read the gap as a defense effect, since teams fight injection hard and fewer clean exploits reach public databases (p. 5). Misinformation runs the other way, near the bottom of the vote and near the top of the record, and is seated in the middle; when fluent, confident output drives a decision or a tool call, a wrong answer becomes a wrong action (p. 5). The leads call the list a consensus product that one noisy year of data should not overturn (p. 5).

The order moved more than in past years (p. 7). Excessive Agency climbed to third, which the list calls the most consequential move, because vote and record agree that agentic deployments are where damage is landing; Unbounded Consumption rose four places; Improper Output Handling fell from fifth to tenth; Prompt Injection and Sensitive Information Disclosure held first and second, the latter being where belief and evidence agree; System Prompt Leakage became Hidden Context Exposure (p. 7). New risks were folded into existing entries rather than new categories: cross-modal attacks into Prompt Injection, promoted model artifacts that are not what they claim into Supply Chain, fine-tuning subversion into Data and Model Poisoning, and assistant-generated insecure code into Improper Output Handling (p. 7). The leads' instruction is to work all ten, starting at the top, and build each for the day the model is turned against you (p. 8).

## Prompt Injection (LLM01)

Prompt injection occurs when any input the model reads (user input, retrieved content, tool output, image, audio or video, intermediate reasoning, persistent memory) alters its behavior against the developer's intent; models do not separate instructions from data, so there is no clean equivalent of parameterized queries (p. 10, citing NCSC, 2025). Context-window pooling, memory persistence and agentic execution make it worse, and an injection can be decomposed by delivery surface, propagation behavior and encoding before choosing mitigations (p. 10). Direct injection may be intentional (jailbreaks) or unintentional; indirect injection arrives through external content on untrusted, semi-trusted or trusted surfaces, and increasingly turns the user's own LLM, such as an MCP-connected agent or developer assistant, against the user's backend, so that the agent, not the attacker, performs the privileged action (pp. 11–12).

Defense is architectural rather than interceptive and works as defense-in-depth: some controls reduce injection success and are expected to degrade against adaptive attackers, others bound the blast radius and survive them; least privilege and capability budgeting are load-bearing for agents (p. 13). Willison's "lethal trifecta" (private data, untrusted content, external communication) is used as a pre-deployment check and Meta AI's Rule of Two as a floor for capability budgeting (pp. 13–14). The eleven controls run from declarative system-prompt constraints, structural output validation, cross-modality filtering and Unicode stripping, through credentials held in application code behind a deterministic policy engine, provenance-labeled channels, human confirmation of the exact rendered action (with invisible-character smuggling and approval fatigue among its limits), and memory writes treated as privileged, to pinned and signed tools and testing against adaptive attackers, where Nasr et al. (2025) found static attack success near zero while adaptive success exceeded 90% for most of 12 recent defenses (pp. 13–15). The nine scenarios include zero-click exfiltration from Microsoft 365 Copilot, the July 2025 Amazon Q incidents, and trusted-backend attacks through a poisoned GitHub issue, Cursor's Supabase MCP server and the malicious postmark-mcp package (pp. 15–17).

## Sensitive Information Disclosure (LLM02)

Disclosure is exposure of confidential, regulated, privileged or proprietary data through any unauthorized channel, including tool-call arguments, reasoning traces, logs, telemetry, embeddings and observable inference properties, each to be treated as output (p. 18). It arises at training, inference, pipeline and observation time; two structural failures drive most incidents: oversharing upstream, whose fix is the data surface rather than the model, and persistence of data in weights, embeddings or adapters after deletion, which strains GDPR and CCPA erasure obligations (p. 18). Severity should turn on what the recipient can learn (p. 19). Examples include training-data extraction, the 2023 ChatGPT Redis bug, embedding inversion (cosine similarity does not respect ACLs), multimodal and side-channel leaks such as Whisper Leak, training-pipeline disclosure, and observability platforms logging full prompts by default (pp. 19–20).

Mitigations follow the DSGAI tiers: foundational controls for every deployment (corpus governance, minimal context, authorization before retrieval, no secrets in system prompts, classifier-based sanitization, query budgets, operational hygiene); hardening for regulated workloads (DP-SGD, vector-store protection, gated log-probabilities, reasoning traces redacted as output, side-channel defenses, join policies); and advanced controls (confidential computing, verifiable erasure, disclosure red-teaming as a release gate, and an incident-response playbook that meets notification obligations) (pp. 20–21). Several of the ten scenarios pair the leak with its regulatory consequence, such as GDPR Article 33 notification or a HIPAA-reportable determination (pp. 21–22).

## Excessive Agency (LLM03)

Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that lets damaging actions follow from unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated LLM outputs, whatever causes the malfunction, with hallucination and prompt injection as common triggers (p. 23). Its root causes are typically excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy, illustrated by tools with unneeded functions, tools left over from development, open-ended shell tools, over-privileged database identities, generic high-privileged identities, and deletions without confirmation (pp. 23–24). Input and output sanitization is not a root control for it (p. 23).

Prevention means minimizing tools, their functionality and their permissions, avoiding open-ended tools, executing tools in the user's context (preserving that context across chained agent calls), requiring user approval for high-impact actions, and complete mediation: authorization in logic, not an LLM's judgment, with graduated enforcement that lets low-consequence or easily reversible actions auto-approve and routes high-consequence or irreversible ones to human review (pp. 24–26). Monitoring and rate limiting with circuit breakers limit damage but do not prevent it (p. 26). The single scenario is an email assistant whose send function lets an injected email have the agent forward sensitive information from the inbox to an attacker (p. 26).

## Supply Chain (LLM04)

LLM supply-chain risk extends beyond code to third-party models, datasets, adapters, conversion and merge workflows, provenance and on-device deployment (p. 27). Examples include vulnerable components and slopsquatting of hallucinated package names, licensing risk, tampered models whose behavioral safety static analysis alone cannot establish, weak provenance and unsigned artifacts, especially those resolved by mutable references, malicious adapters and quantization-triggered behavior, on-device tampering, and unclear supplier terms (pp. 28–29).

Mitigations are supplier vetting, A06:2021-style patching, red teaming of selected models, signed SBOM/AIBOM inventories, and signing with transparency logs, while recognizing that signing proves integrity and origin, not safety, so it is combined with immutable references, release gates, behavioral evaluation and continuous validation (p. 30). The scenarios cover compromised packages and serving frameworks, tampered hub models, adapter and conversion-service compromise, namespace reuse, scanner and safe-format bypasses, a compromised build pipeline whose artifact, built and signed by the organization's own release infrastructure, passes downstream provenance checks, and a re-packaged mobile app (pp. 31–32).

## Data and Model Poisoning (LLM05)

Poisoning embeds harmful behavior, bias or exploitable weaknesses through manipulated data or model artifacts anywhere data is ingested, transformed, retrieved or reused; it targets the model's learning process, and fixing it can mean revalidation, retraining, replacement or pipeline redesign (p. 33). Bundled artifacts such as chat templates, tokenizer configs, adapters and pickle files can carry backdoors that leave behavior untouched until a trigger, creating the opportunity for a model to become a sleeper agent (p. 34). As few as 250 poisoned documents can compromise models from 600M to 13B parameters (Souly et al., 2025), and a single optimized poisoned text per targeted query can override accurate RAG content (Zhang et al., 2025) (pp. 34–35).

The twelve mitigations include lineage tracking and signing, strict validation of incoming data, RAG trust boundaries, anomaly and drift detection, data version control, controlled retraining loops, trigger-probing after every alignment cycle (safety alignment is not to be assumed to remove backdoors), and treating inference artifacts as security-relevant code (pp. 35–36). Scenarios range from poisoned knowledge repositories and feedback loops to a chat-template backdoor that cut factual accuracy from 90% to 15% under trigger (Fogel et al., 2026) and persistent agent-memory poisoning (pp. 36–37).

## Unbounded Consumption (LLM06)

Unbounded Consumption is uncontrolled inference that lets attackers disrupt availability, inflict costs or clone a model; a defining characteristic is cost asymmetry, and reasoning models, multimodal inputs, agentic tool fan-out and shared inference infrastructure compound it, so request-rate limiting alone no longer suffices (p. 38). Examples include input floods and output explosion, Denial of Wallet, near-limit context abuse, reasoning-loop exhaustion, sponge examples, multimodal token costs, model extraction, recursive tool-calling loops, and serving-framework exploits (pp. 38–39).

Controls include token- and cost-aware rate limits with pre-flight estimation, hard spending caps that halt inference rather than alert, sandboxing, graceful degradation, queue limits, perturbation scanning, tool-interaction baselines, agentic circuit breakers (step, recursion, time and cost limits, with state hashing), and hardened inference infrastructure (pp. 40–41). One scenario shows per-turn cost in a long agentic session climbing from about $0.001 to about $0.50 by turn 100 without any single request tripping a limit (p. 42).

## Misinformation (LLM07)

Misinformation is incorrect, incomplete, unsupported or misleading output that appears credible enough to influence a human decision, a workflow or an agent action; the core risk is that it is trusted and acted on, and because outputs now drive tool calls, code, state and authorization, it is a system-level failure (p. 43). Overreliance is a key factor and, in agentic architectures, is often built into system design (p. 43). Examples include false decision support, incorrect state inference, hallucinated dependencies, misleading summaries and omissions, adversarially induced falsehoods, cross-agent propagation, and forged evidence (pp. 43–44).

Prevention grounds claims before action, separates generation from execution (Claim-Check-Act), validates tool calls against current state, uses verification signals beyond confidence alone, such as groundedness and consistency checks, requires runtime verification for high-impact actions, demands structured outputs with mandatory fields, limits blast radius, logs claims and outcomes, and calibrates trust (p. 44). The scenarios include a wrongly approved refund, an omitted drug contraindication, a false alert that blocks a production network segment, a payment agent trusting an unverified identity state, and a backup reported complete that never ran (p. 45).

## Hidden Context Exposure (LLM08)

Hidden Context Exposure, which replaces System Prompt Leakage, is the unauthorized extraction, inference or reconstruction of non-user-facing instructions and context (system prompt, developer instructions, retrieved policy, tool schemas), security-relevant when that context contains or reveals details that materially increase attacker capability (pp. 7, 46). Practitioners should assume hidden context is discoverable and not secret, keep credentials out of it, and never rely on it alone as a security boundary; severity runs from informational to critical according to what is placed there and how the application relies on it (p. 46). Exposure amplifies prompt injection, information disclosure, excessive agency and improper output handling (p. 46).

Examples cover leaked tool schemas and credentials, behavioral control logic, refusal mechanisms, permissions and roles, and output-format rules (pp. 47–48). Mitigation keeps sensitive data out of hidden context, enforces critical behavior through deterministic systems outside the model, and enforces authorization independently of the LLM (p. 48).

## Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (LLM09)

Wherever similarity search sits between a data source and the prompt, the embedding layer is part of the trust boundary; these attacks exploit embedding geometry, and many succeed when the retrieved content carries no malicious instructions at all (p. 50). The entry's frame: poisoning makes the system wrong, inversion makes it leak, jamming makes it silent, and access-control failure makes it indiscriminate (p. 50). Examples are cross-tenant leakage when search runs before access control, embedding inversion (so an embeddings-only leak is a document leak), retrieval-time poisoning, retrieval jamming with a single blocker document, membership inference, semantic-cache and deduplication poisoning, and multimodal embedding poisoning (pp. 50–52).

Mitigations enforce tenant scope inside the index query (a client-supplied scope is a suggestion, not a control), validate and track provenance for every embedding, segregate trust tiers by index, detect anomalies at ingest and retrieval, manage the storage lifecycle (deletion, backups at source sensitivity, re-embedding on model rotation), and keep immutable retrieval logs with incident playbooks that treat embedding leaks as source-data leaks (pp. 52–53).

## Improper Output Handling (LLM10)

Improper Output Handling is insufficient validation, sanitization and handling of output before it passes downstream; because prompt input can control output, it is like giving users indirect access to extra functionality, and it can yield XSS, CSRF, SSRF, privilege escalation or remote code execution (p. 55). Conditions that raise impact include excess privilege, indirect injection, missing context-specific encoding, terminal sinks that interpret control characters, and client renderers that auto-fetch referenced resources (p. 55).

Mitigation treats the model like any other user under zero trust: ASVS-guided validation, context-aware output encoding, parameterized queries, strict CSP, monitoring, control-character sanitization, and no automatic outbound fetches from rendered output (pp. 56–57). Scenarios include an unvalidated response reaching a tool with administrative functions, SQL and JavaScript sinks, exfiltration through a summarizer, and LLM-generated code deployed without review (p. 57).

## Framework Mappings (Appendix A)

Appendix A replaces the per-entry framework sections with one version-pinned reference mapping the ten entries to the OWASP Agentic Top 10 (ASI), OWASP GenAI Data Security (DSGAI), MITRE ATLAS, MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE CWE, NIST AI 600-1, NIST AI RMF, the CSA AI Controls Matrix and OWASP AIVSS, marking each element primary or supporting (p. 58). A coverage matrix shows every pairing mapped except LLM02 with AIVSS and LLM10 with the NIST AI RMF (pp. 58–59). Each framework section defines its own primary/supporting split, and the appendix lists element-level mappings with a relevance note for each (pp. 59–105).

## Key Statistics

- Incident corpus: 7,714 incidents; 6,639 classified; vote weighted three-quarters, incident data one quarter (p. 5).
- Adaptive attacks exceeded 90% success against most of 12 defenses whose static success was near zero (Nasr et al., 2025) (LLM01, p. 15).
- Five poisoned documents reached roughly 90% attack success against a knowledge base of millions of texts (W. Zou et al., 2025) (LLM01, pp. 15–16).
- A divergence attack extracted more than 10,000 memorized examples from gpt-3.5-turbo for roughly USD 200 (Nasr et al., 2023) (LLM02, p. 19).
- 250 poisoned documents compromised models from 600M to 13B parameters (Souly et al., 2025) (LLM05, p. 34).
- A chat-template backdoor cut factual accuracy from 90% to 15% under trigger across 18 models (Fogel et al., 2026) (LLM05, p. 36).
- Agentic session cost grew from about $0.001 to about $0.50 per turn by turn 100 (LLM06, p. 42).
- Vec2Text reconstructed 92% of short 32-token inputs exactly (Morris et al., 2023) (LLM09, p. 51).

## Key Connections

- The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, which takes over where the model becomes an actor (pp. 7, 59–63).
- OWASP GenAI Data Security 2026, whose tiers structure LLM02's mitigations (pp. 20, 64–68).
- Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" and Meta AI's Rule of Two, used as capability checks for agents; Noma Security on the rule's silence about autonomy depth (pp. 13–14).
- NCSC, NIST AI 100-2 E2025 and Debenedetti et al., cited for the absence of reliable prompt-injection prevention (pp. 10, 13).
- Nasr et al. (2025) on adaptive attacks defeating published defenses (pp. 13–15).
- OWASP A06:2021, ASVS, CycloneDX ML-BOM and the AIBOM project; OpenSSF Model Signing, Sigstore, CoSAI and SLSA (pp. 28, 30, 56).
- MITRE ATLAS, ATT&CK and CWE; NIST AI 600-1 and the AI RMF; the CSA AI Controls Matrix; OWASP AIVSS (pp. 58–105).
- EU AI Act, GDPR, HIPAA, CCPA/CPRA and ISO/IEC 42001 as applicable regimes (pp. 18–22).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Building a model that cannot be fooled is the wrong goal; build the system so a fooled model breaks nothing important (p. 5).
2. One noisy year of incident data should not overturn practitioner judgment, and thin new categories would splinter the list (pp. 5, 7).
3. Prompt-injection defense is architectural, not interceptive, and static-only attack-success claims should be rejected (LLM01, pp. 13, 15).
4. Authorization must not be left to the model or to hidden context (LLM03, p. 25; LLM08, pp. 46, 48).
5. An "embeddings-only" leak is not low-severity: embeddings can be inverted to source text (LLM02, p. 19; LLM09, p. 54).
6. Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety; safety alignment should not be assumed to remove backdoors (LLM04, p. 30; LLM05, p. 35).
7. Request-rate limiting alone is no longer sufficient, and hard caps should halt rather than alert (LLM06, pp. 38, 40).
8. Confidence alone is not a verification signal (LLM07, p. 44).
